displayQuote: This would be the best of all possible worlds, if there were no religion in it

meta.title: Who really said "This would be the best of all possible worlds, if there were no religion in it"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: John Adams did write it, in an 1817 letter to Jefferson. In the next breath he rejected it: without religion, he wrote, the world would be "Hell."
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'This would be the best of all possible worlds, if there were no religion in it'?
meta.ogDescription: Real Adams words, quoted backwards. In his 19 April 1817 letter to Jefferson he called the thought fanatical. Without religion, he said, the world would be Hell.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1735–1826 · Second President of the United States
answer.sourceLine: This comes from Adams’s letter to Thomas Jefferson, Quincy, 19 April 1817, and it is confirmed in the manuscript transcription. He says he was tempted to “break out” with this line, then rejects it at once: “Without Religion this World would be Something not fit to be mentioned in polite Company, I mean Hell.”

source.heading: The letter it comes from

docMeta.dd: Letter, John Adams to Thomas Jefferson
The Works of John Adams, vol. 10 (Boston: Little, Brown, 1856), p. 254

source.excerpt: One day, when the Schoolmaster had been more than commonly fanatical, and declared “if he were a Monark, He would have but one Religion in his Dominions” The Parson coolly replied “Cleverly! You would be the best Man in the World, if you had no Religion.” Twenty times, in the course of my late Reading, have I been upon the point of breaking out, “This would be the best of all possible Worlds, if there were no Religion in it”!!! But in this exclamati[on] I Should have been as fanatical as Bryant or Cleverly. Without Religion this World would be Something not fit to be mentioned in polite Company, I mean Hell.
trail: The full letter is transcribed from the manuscript in The Papers of Thomas Jefferson, Retirement Series, vol. 11, on Founders Online ↗. The edition places the original at the Library of Congress.
Adams’s grandson Charles Francis Adams printed the letter in The Works of John Adams, vol. 10 (1856), p. 254 ↗. That edition reads “if there was no religion in it ! ! !”
Jefferson quoted the line back in his reply of 5 May 1817 ↗. He agreed with it only if “religion” meant “Sectarian dogmas.”
Wikiquote’s John Adams page ↗ lists the passage as sourced to this letter and warns that the italicized part “has often been quoted out of context.” We found no Quote Investigator article on it.
source.excerptNote: This is the manuscript spelling and capitalization as transcribed in The Papers of Thomas Jefferson, Retirement Series, vol. 11. “Bryant” is Lemuel Bryant, Adams’s boyhood parish priest, and “Cleverly” is Joseph Cleverly, his Latin schoolmaster. Both are introduced earlier in the same letter.

author.name: John Adams
author.heading: About John Adams
author.bio: John Adams was a Massachusetts lawyer and revolutionary leader. He became the second President of the United States (1797–1801). In retirement at Quincy he kept up a long and famously frank exchange of letters with his old rival Thomas Jefferson, full of reading, religion and philosophy. The 1817 letter quoted here is part of that exchange.

misattribution.heading: Real words, reversed meaning
misattribution.intro: This is not a fake quote. It is a clipped one. Adams wrote the sentence only to say he had been tempted to blurt it out, and then he called that temptation fanatical. Popular versions stop before his answer.

items.who: Stand-alone versions credited to John Adams
items.why: Quotewise ↗ shows the line by itself, ending at “religion in it,” with no sign that Adams went on to reject it.
Goodreads ↗ gives the “Twenty times” lead-in but ends at the exclamation. It leaves out the sentences in which Adams calls the thought fanatical and says a world without religion would be “Hell.”
The Works of John Adams, vol. 10 ↗ prints “if there was no religion in it.” The manuscript, as transcribed in the Jefferson Papers ↗, reads “were.” The popular version follows the manuscript.

misattribution.truthLine: Adams did write the line, but as a thought he turned down: “in this exclamati[on] I Should have been as fanatical as Bryant or Cleverly. Without Religion this World would be Something not fit to be mentioned in polite Company, I mean Hell.” (letter of 19 April 1817 ↗)

context.heading: Why it matters
lead: The line is set up by a story from Adams’s boyhood. His schoolmaster, Joseph Cleverly, said that as a monarch he would allow only one religion. The parish priest, Lemuel Bryant, answered: “Cleverly! You would be the best Man in the World, if you had no Religion.” Adams then admits he has often wanted to say the same of the whole world, and immediately calls that urge as fanatical as either man. The editors of the Jefferson Papers note that “best of all possible worlds” echoes Leibniz.

Jefferson read it the same way. In his reply of 5 May 1817 ↗ he wrote that if religion meant “Sectarian dogmas” the exclamation was “just.” If it meant shared moral precepts, then without it the world would be, “as you again say, ‘something not fit to be named, even indeed a Hell.’”
detailsBody: Adams goes on: “So far from believing in the total and universal depravity of human Nature; I believe there is no Individual totally depraved. … while Conscience remains there is Some Religion.” The Library of Congress shows the holograph letter ↗ in its exhibition Religion and the Founding of the American Republic, where it quotes the “Hell” sentence.
